old: He doubted whether to embrace him
new: He did not know whether to embrace him
reason: This is a dead sense. Today 'doubt whether' means to question whether something is so, so 'He doubted whether to embrace him' reads as reluctance to embrace his father. Butler's sense is being torn between two courses, which the 'or whether' that follows spells out. No current modern Book keeps Butler's 'doubted whether'. The same construction ('he doubted whether to …, or to …') is printed 'he did not know whether to …, or to …' at 4.9. 6.11 prints 'did not know what to do' (GLOSSARY Book 5/6 table, B06-P012) and 10.11 'was uncertain whether'. 'did not know whether' follows 4.9 exactly and leaves GLOSSARY's reserved 'still undecided' alone. Three words replace two, and every clause stays in Butler's order. The reader recovered, so this is optional.

old: but bears the trace of your attention
new: that does not bear the trace of your attention
reason: This is obsolete syntax that can invert the sense. 'not a single X … but bears' (meaning 'that does not bear') is no longer current English, where 'but' reads as 'except' or as a contrast. So the sentence can be taken as 'no plant bears the trace of your attention', the opposite of Odysseus's compliment. 'that does not bear' is the current form of the same double negative. Every item Butler lists stays, in his order, and nothing is added or dropped. The next sentence ('you take better care of your garden than of yourself') lets an attentive reader recover, so this is optional. The accepted record already modernized the same class at 23.11 (Butler's 'even though he was not one who would leave many friends').

old: with corn planted between each row
new: with grain planted between each row
reason: This is a transatlantic false friend. Butler's British 'corn' means grain in general. This edition is American English throughout (GLOSSARY spelling standard), and in American English 'corn' is maize, a New World crop. So the ordinary reader pictures maize growing between Laertes's vines and never notices that anything is wrong. The package has already made this rendering: 3.36 prints 'the grain lands of the open country' for Butler's 'the corn lands'. One word changes and nothing is added. Butler's claim that a crop was sown between the vine rows stands.

This is a false friend, and the proposal keeps one Butler phrase to one rendering across Books. Of a person's build, current 'stout' chiefly means portly, so as Athena gives Laertes 'a more imposing presence', a typical reader has her make him fatter. Butler means solidly built (the Greek comparative is 'thicker-set, sturdier'), and 'sturdier' keeps his meaning and his comparative. The Book 8 adjudication proposes the same change for Butler's same phrase at 8.1 (B08-01, 'taller and sturdier', optional) and names 24.23 as the other instance. Apply this together with B08-01 or not at all, so that one Butler phrase keeps one rendering. It is optional because the reader recovered. Butler's different phrase at 23.15, 'taller and stronger', is left alone and stays distinct.

old: offer his bow and a quantity of iron to be competed for by us ill-fated suitors
new: offer his bow and a quantity of iron as a contest for us ill-fated suitors
reason: The blind reader misread this: 'a quantity of iron to be competed for reads like a prize, and then "sent his arrow through the iron" makes no sense.' Butler's 'to be contended for' is ambiguous between prize and contest. Homer's word (24.169, aethlia) means the bow and the iron are the means of the contest, the axe-heads the arrow must pass through. The adjudicator kept it as Butler's own wording. The lead repairs it, because it is one of the review's few genuine misreads and the fix adds no gloss in Amphimedon's speech: 'as a contest for us' names what the iron is for without explaining the axes. Butler's 24.10 has 'contended' only, so no 'contest' collides.
